summary.text: Maxwell's equations are a set of equations describing how electric and magnetic fields are produced by electric charges and currents.
Together with the Lorentz force law they underpin classical electromagnetism, optics and circuits, and they model technologies such as motors, radio and radar.
Maxwell's key addition, that changing electric fields also produce magnetic fields, predicts self-sustaining waves whose speed matches that of light.

facts.value: James Clerk Maxwell, who published an early form in 1861-62

facts.label: Equation count
facts.value: Four equations determine the fields from charges and currents

facts.label: What it unified
facts.value: Magnetism, electricity, light and related radiation

facts.label: Known limit
facts.value: A classical limit of quantum electrodynamics

items.prompt: A bar magnet is spun next to a loop of wire. According to the Maxwell-Faraday law, what does the changing magnetic field do?

options.label: It makes the wire magnetic
It cancels any electric field nearby
It makes the wire heavier
It generates an electric field in the wire

items.explain: A time-varying magnetic field goes with an electric field; this induction is how many generators work.

items.prompt: You cut a bar magnet in half hoping to get one piece with only a north pole. What do Maxwell's equations say about the pieces?

options.label: Each piece is still a dipole with two poles
One piece is north only and the other south only
Both pieces lose their magnetism completely
The pieces repel each other until they separate

items.explain: Gauss's law for magnetism says no isolated north or south poles exist; a magnet's field comes from a dipole.

items.prompt: Ampère's original law tied magnetic fields to electric current. What did Maxwell add to it?

options.label: Magnetic fields vanish when current stops
Magnetic fields also come from changing electric fields
Current only flows if a magnetic field is present
Magnetic fields are always steady in time

items.explain: Maxwell's addition, called displacement current, says that magnetic fields also relate to changing electric fields.

items.prompt: What clue led Maxwell to conclude that light is a kind of electromagnetic wave?

options.label: Light and the waves both bend around corners
Both need a material like air to travel through
The calculated wave speed matched the measured speed of light
Both were first seen in experiments with magnets

items.explain: The speed calculated for the waves, predictable from experiments on charges and currents, matches the speed of light.

items.prompt: A tiny speck in empty space carries a negative charge. Which way does the electric field around it point?

options.label: Toward the speck
Away from the speck
In circles around the speck
Straight up, whatever the charge

items.explain: By Gauss's law, an electric field points away from positive charges and toward negative ones.

items.prompt: An engineer designing a transformer uses the version of the equations for large-scale matter instead of tracking every atom. What is the trade-off?

options.label: It is exact but only works in empty space
It needs atom-by-atom charge data as input
It works only for static fields, never changing ones
It is easier to use but needs measured material parameters

items.explain: The macroscopic equations avoid atomic-scale charges, but they require experimentally determined parameters for how materials respond.

beats.title: Light Was Hiding in the Equations
beats.hook: Maxwell worked out a wave from pure electricity and magnetism, and its speed was already famous.

beats.prompt: Maxwell's equations allow electric and magnetic fields to sustain each other as a wave through empty space. What speed do they give for it?
beats.explain: The calculated speed, predictable from experiments on charges and currents, matches the speed of light, so light is an electromagnetic wave.

choices.label: Infinite, so the wave arrives instantly
choices.feedback: The calculation gives a finite number, and it is a famous one.

choices.label: Whatever speed its source happens to move
choices.feedback: The speed comes out of the equations, using constants measured from charges and currents.

beats.prompt: match each law to what it says

right.label: No isolated north or south pole exists
Electric fields point away from positive charges and toward negative ones
A changing magnetic field goes with an electric field
Currents and changing electric fields go with a magnetic field

beats.explain: Together these four statements describe how charges, currents and changing fields produce electric and magnetic fields.

beats.prompt: put these steps of Maxwell's reasoning in order

items.label: Ampere's law ties magnetic fields to electric current
Maxwell adds that changing electric fields also make magnetic fields
So changing fields can sustain each other as a wave through empty space
The wave's speed matches light, so light is an electromagnetic wave

beats.explain: Maxwell's addition to Ampere's law implies self-sustaining waves, and their speed identifies them as light.

beats.prompt: one step in this reasoning is wrong; which?

steps.text: Gauss's law for magnetism says electric charges have no magnetic analogues.
So a north pole cannot exist on its own.
A magnet's field is instead attributed to a dipole.
So the net outflow of magnetic field through a closed surface is positive.

beats.explain: For a dipole the net outflow of the magnetic field through any closed surface is zero.

beats.idea: Changing electric and magnetic fields can sustain each other as a wave, and that wave is light.

paragraphs.heading: What they are
paragraphs.text: Maxwell's equations are a set of linked equations that describe how electric charges and currents produce electric and magnetic fields. Combined with the Lorentz force law, they underpin classical electromagnetism and classical optics, as well as electric and magnetic circuits. They give the mathematical model behind power generation, electric motors, wireless communication, lenses and radar.

paragraphs.heading: Gauss's two laws
paragraphs.text: Gauss's law links the electric field to electric charges. The field points away from positive charges and toward negative ones, and the total field flowing out through a closed surface is proportional to the charge inside it. Gauss's law for magnetism says there are no magnetic monopoles: no north or south pole ever exists on its own. Instead, the magnetic field of a material is put down to a dipole, and the net magnetic field flowing out through any closed surface is zero.

paragraphs.heading: Faraday's law
paragraphs.text: Another equation, a version of Faraday's law of induction, ties a magnetic field that changes in time to an electric field. In its integral form, it says the work per unit charge needed to carry a charge around a closed loop equals how fast the magnetic flux through that loop is changing. This electromagnetic induction is how many electric generators work. A spinning bar magnet, for example, makes a changing magnetic field, which in turn produces an electric field in a wire nearby.

paragraphs.heading: Maxwell's addition
paragraphs.text: Another equation starts from Ampère's original law, which ties magnetic fields to electric current. Maxwell added that magnetic fields are also tied to changing electric fields, which he called displacement current. One result is that a changing electric field comes with a rotating magnetic field. Another is that electromagnetic waves can sustain themselves and travel through empty space. Experiments on charges and currents let you predict how fast these waves go, and the answer matches the speed of light, and light is indeed one kind of electromagnetic radiation, as are X-rays and radio waves.

paragraphs.heading: Who wrote them
paragraphs.text: They take their name from James Clerk Maxwell, a physicist and mathematician who published an early form in 1861 and 1862. That work united magnetism, electricity, light and related radiation, which until then had been described separately. In 1861 Maxwell saw the link between electromagnetic waves and light, joining electromagnetism and optics. The modern, most common form is credited to Oliver Heaviside. His vector calculus version became the standard, and it is clearer than Maxwell's original 20 equations written out in x, y and z components.

paragraphs.heading: Versions and limits
paragraphs.text: Two versions are used most. The microscopic equations apply everywhere, but they work with the total charge and current, down to the messy charges and currents inside atoms, which makes them clumsy for everyday calculations. The macroscopic equations bring in two extra fields that describe matter on a large scale without tracking atoms, though they need properties of materials measured by experiment. Since the mid-20th century, physicists have understood that Maxwell's equations are not exact. They are the classical limit of a more precise theory, quantum electrodynamics.
